title: Read a Real Bug Bounty Programme

content.objective: Read a real, published bug bounty programme or vulnerability disclosure policy from a major technology company. Identify the exact provisions that create legal protection for researchers — scope, safe harbour, prohibited actions, and the disclosure process — so you understand what a professional framework looks like in practice.
instructions: Navigate to one of the following bug bounty or disclosure programmes: HackerOne (hackerone.com/directory — search for a large company), Bugcrowd (bugcrowd.com/programs), Google (bughunters.google.com), Microsoft (msrc.microsoft.com), or GitHub (github.com/security). Choose a programme from a company you recognise.

Find and read the full programme policy document — not just the reward table. Look specifically for: (a) the scope section listing in-scope and out-of-scope targets, (b) the list of prohibited testing techniques, (c) the safe harbour or legal protection clause, and (d) the process for submitting a report.
Identify whether the programme has a safe harbour clause. If it does, write down what it promises the researcher. If it does not, note that absence.
Find one specific prohibited action that surprised you — something you might have assumed was acceptable but is explicitly forbidden. Consider why the company may have prohibited it.
Review the reward structure (if the programme offers financial rewards). What is the maximum reward for a Critical severity vulnerability? What criteria determine severity?
successCriteria: You have read the full programme policy for one published bug bounty or vulnerability disclosure programme and can name the company and where the policy is hosted.
You can describe what is in scope and what is out of scope for the programme — including at least one example of each.
You can state whether the programme has a safe harbour clause, and if so, what it commits the organisation to.
You have identified at least one prohibited action and can explain why it is prohibited.
You can describe the process a researcher must follow to submit a valid vulnerability report under this programme.
content.reflection: Security researchers who operate within published bug bounty programmes are the 'white hat' version of grey hat curiosity: same skill, same discovery, but with a legal framework that protects both sides. As you read the programme you chose, notice how precisely written the scope and prohibited actions are. Every prohibited item is there because someone — possibly multiple researchers — did it without permission, and the programme owner had to deal with the consequences. The programme document is essentially a history of where the lines were drawn, and why.
